titre_video: Military Conspiracies That Sound 100% Fake but Were True

segments.titre: Intro: military conspiracy theories that turned out true
segments.resume: Opening hook: the military denied for decades that it ran false flags, poisoned soldiers or operated psychic spy units, yet the so-called tin foil hat theories were right. Sets up a countdown of 29 real military conspiracies.
segments.texte: Every tin foil hat theory you’ve heard… might actually be true. For decades, the military gaslit anyone who said they were conducting false flags, poisoning soldiers or running psychic spy units. Turns out, the crazies were right.

segments.titre: No. 29: Operation Popeye, weather warfare over Vietnam
segments.resume: From 1967 to 1972 the US Air Force flew over 2,600 cloud-seeding sorties over Laos and Vietnam with silver iodide to extend the monsoon and turn the Ho Chi Minh Trail into mud (motto: make mud, not war). Journalist Jack Anderson exposed it in 1971, a Senate hearing confirmed it in 1974, and a 1977 treaty banned weather warfare.
segments.texte: 29: For 5 years, one of the most classified weapons over Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh Trail was the rain. Under Operation Popeye, Air Force crews flew more than 2,600 cloud-seeding sorties over Laos and Vietnam between 1967 and 1972, pumping silver iodide into monsoon clouds. The goal was to stretch the rainy season by up to 45 days and turn North Vietnam's supply roads into rivers of mud. The crews even had an unofficial motto, make mud, not war. For years, anyone who claimed the US was controlling the weather sounded unhinged. Then journalist Jack Anderson exposed the program in 1971, and in 1974 a Senate hearing confirmed it. The fallout was such that the world actually signed a treaty in 1977 specifically banning weather warfare. Which means that, somewhere in international law, there's a rule that exists because the Air Force tried to weaponize a cloud.

segments.titre: No. 28: Stargate and the remote viewing program
segments.resume: For about two decades the Army, DIA and CIA spent roughly $20 million on remote viewing experiments (last codename Stargate, based at Fort Meade) to locate hostages, Soviet facilities and missing aircraft. A 1995 independent review found it never produced a single piece of actionable intelligence.
segments.texte: 28. For 2 decades, a slice of America’s intelligence budget went to men sitting in dark rooms at Fort Meade, Maryland. This wasn’t some secret listening station, they were trying to see the Soviet Union… with their eyes closed. Under a rotating cast of codenames, the last and most famous being Stargate, the Army, the Defense Intelligence Agency, and the CIA spent roughly $20 million on “remote viewing” experiments from the 1970s until 1995. Viewers were tasked with locating hostages, Soviet weapons facilities, and missing aircraft. Basically anything the satellites couldn't catch. When the CIA had the program independently reviewed in 1995, the verdict was that it had never produced a single piece of intelligence anyone could act on. 20 years and $20 million later, the CIA’s psychics couldn’t find anything foreign militaries were hiding. Which is ironic, because their own military was hiding entire bases under the ice.

segments.titre: No. 27: Camp Century and Project Iceworm in Greenland
segments.resume: In 1959 the Army unveiled Camp Century, research tunnels in the Greenland ice sheet powered by a portable nuclear reactor. The hidden plan, Project Iceworm, was to base up to 600 nuclear missiles there despite Denmark's nuclear ban. The moving ice crushed the tunnels and the Army left behind fuel, sewage and radioactive waste that may resurface as the ice melts.
segments.texte: 27. In 1959, the Army unveiled Camp Century, a warren of scientific research tunnels dug into the Greenland ice sheet and powered by a portable nuclear reactor. It was a PR dream. They even flew in an American and a Danish Boy Scout to intern at the base for six months. What the world didn't see was the real plan behind everything. Project Iceworm, a scheme to carve thousands of miles of tunnels through the ice and hide up to 600 nuclear missiles within striking range of the Soviet Union. The problem? Greenland technically belonged to Denmark, and Denmark officially banned nuclear weapons on its soil. The truth didn't fully come out until a Danish government investigation in the 1990s. The ice ended up winning out, too. Glaciers moved, and the tunnels began crushing themselves within a few years. So the Army left. It also left behind tons of its diesel fuel, sewage, and radioactive waste, which scientists now think could resurface as the ice melts. If you thought leaving nuclear waste for future generations was bad, on the other side of the Iron Curtain, the Soviets had nuclear waste of their own to dispose of.

segments.titre: No. 26: the Kyshtym nuclear disaster at Mayak (1957)
segments.resume: On September 29, 1957 a radioactive waste tank exploded at the Mayak plutonium complex in the Urals, contaminating thousands of square miles and forcing about 10,000 evacuations. It is named after Kyshtym because Mayak's own city officially did not exist. Rated level 6 on the INES scale, it was revealed by Zhores Medvedev in 1976 and admitted by Moscow only in 1989.
segments.texte: 26. The worst nuclear disaster most people have never heard of is named after the wrong town. On September 29th, 1957, a cooling system failed on an underground tank of radioactive waste at the Mayak plutonium complex in the Ural Mountains. The tank exploded, and the blast spread radioactive contamination across thousands of square miles. Around 10,000 people were evacuated, many never told why. Entire villages were bulldozed and removed from maps. The disaster is named after the nearby town of Kyshtym for one reason; Mayak's own city didn't officially exist. The disaster was rated a level 6 on the international nuclear accident scale. Only Chernobyl and Fukushima rank higher. The world only heard about it when exiled Soviet scientist Zhores Medvedev wrote about it in 1976. Moscow didn't officially admit a thing about it until 1989, 32 years later. Losing track of radioactive material is one thing. But what about that time an entire ship full of uranium just…disappeared?

segments.titre: No. 25: Perimeter, the Soviet Dead Hand doomsday machine
segments.resume: Operational by 1985, the Soviet Perimeter system, nicknamed Dead Hand, detected nuclear blasts and, if contact with leadership was lost, let officers in a bunker launch command rockets broadcasting launch orders to surviving silos. Compared to the doomsday machine in Dr. Strangelove, it was confirmed after the Cold War and reportedly remains in service.
segments.texte: 25. The plot of the 1960s film Dr. Strangelove hinges on the Soviets building an automatic doomsday machine and neglecting to tell anyone. 2 decades later, the real Soviet Union built almost exactly that and neglected to tell anyone, either. The system was called Perimeter, but it's better known by its nickname, Dead Hand. Operational by 1985, it used sensors to detect nuclear blasts on Soviet soil. If it registered a blast and lost contact with the military leadership, officers in a deep bunker could launch special command rockets. They would fly across the country, broadcasting launch orders to every surviving missile silo. In other words, killing the Kremlin wouldn't stop the Kremlin's missiles. Western analysts spent years dismissing rumors of the system before its existence was confirmed after the Cold War. Russian officials have indicated it's still in service today. While the Soviets were wiring up the end of the world, the US Navy was sitting on the bottom of the ocean, listening…

segments.titre: No. 24: Operation Ivy Bells, tapping a Soviet cable in the Sea of Okhotsk
segments.resume: In 1971 the submarine USS Halibut found a Soviet undersea communications cable in the Sea of Okhotsk, and Navy divers clamped a six-ton recording pod on it that picked up calls without cutting the line. The Soviets barely encrypted their talk; the operation ended in 1980 when NSA analyst Ronald Pelton sold the secret for about $35,000.
segments.texte: 24. The Sea of Okhotsk was basically the Soviet Union’s private lake during the Cold War. Which is exactly why, in 1971, the submarine USS Halibut slipped into it hunting for an undersea communications cable. They found it the low-tech way, by spotting signs on the shoreline warning ships not to anchor there. Working 400 feet (122 meters) underwater, Navy divers attached a recording pod roughly 20 feet (6 meters) long and weighing six tons to the cable, which picked up conversations without even cutting into it. Soviet officers assumed nobody could reach that cable, so they barely bothered encrypting what they said. For years, American subs covertly returned to swap out the tapes. Operation Ivy Bells ended in 1980, when a broke NSA analyst named Ronald Pelton walked into the Soviet embassy and sold the whole secret for about $35,000. Selling out made Pelton a traitor. But the CIA found its own ways to sell secrets…back to themselves.

segments.titre: No. 23: Crypto AG, the encryption company secretly owned by the CIA
segments.resume: Around 120 governments bought encryption machines from Swiss firm Crypto AG, which since 1970 was secretly owned by the CIA and West German intelligence, who rigged the machines. Under Operation Rubicon the US read Iran's messages during the hostage crisis and passed Argentina's to Britain in the Falklands War; the scheme was exposed only in 2020.
segments.texte: 23. Imagine buying the best safe money can buy, then finding out the manufacturer kept a copy of every key. Now imagine you’re 120 countries doing that exact same thing. For decades, if a government wanted to keep its secrets safe, it bought its encryption machines from Crypto AG, a company based in neutral Switzerland. Nations trusted it with their most sensitive military and diplomatic messages. What they didn't know was that, since 1970, Crypto AG had been secretly owned by the CIA and West German intelligence. And they rigged the machines so the messages could be cracked. Under Operation Rubicon, US spies read Iran's communications during the hostage crisis and fed Argentina's military messages to Britain during the Falklands War. And the best part? The targets were paying for the privilege, which makes this one of the few intelligence operations in history that also turned a profit. A CIA historian called it "the intelligence coup of the century." It wasn’t until 2020, that the whole thing was exposed.. Messages are one thing. But the CIA also wanted to steal a Soviet submarine… while it was 3 miles (4.8 km) underwater.

segments.titre: No. 22: Project Azorian and the raising of Soviet sub K-129
segments.resume: After the Soviet submarine K-129 sank in 1968, the CIA found it over 16,000 feet down and built the Glomar Explorer, cover-storied as a Howard Hughes ocean mining ship, with a giant claw to lift it. In 1974 the claw broke and only part of the sub rose, with six sailors buried at sea; the episode gave rise to the CIA's "Glomar response" (neither confirm nor deny).
segments.texte: 22. In 1968, the Soviet submarine K-129 sank in the Pacific with 98 men and nuclear missiles aboard. The Soviets never found it, but the US did, more than 16,000 feet (4,877 meters) down. So the CIA built a massive ship with a giant mechanical claw hidden inside to reach down and grab it. Their cover story was that eccentric billionaire Howard Hughes was building the Glomar Explorer to mine the ocean floor for minerals. When Howard Hughes was mentioned, nobody batted an eyelid. In 1974, Project Azorian actually worked. Well, partly. The claw broke mid-lift, and only a section of the sub made it up. Inside were the bodies of 6 Soviet sailors, whom the CIA buried at sea with full military honors. When reporters started asking questions, the CIA replied that it could neither confirm nor deny anything. That phrase is still called the “Glomar response” today. It remains the CIA’s answer of choice for most questions they’re asked.

segments.titre: No. 21: France's bombing of the Rainbow Warrior
segments.resume: In July 1985 two bombs sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland as it prepared to protest French nuclear tests; photographer Fernando Pereira drowned. Two DGSE agents posing as a Swiss honeymoon couple were arrested; France denied it for months, then admitted it, the Defense Minister resigned and the agents served about two years.
segments.texte: 21. Most governments used to respond to Greenpeace protestors with a strongly-worded statement. France decided to tell off the environmental activists with bombs. In July 1985, the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior was docked in Auckland, New Zealand, preparing to sail out and protest French nuclear tests in the Pacific. Just before midnight, 2 bombs tore through its hull. Photographer Fernando Pereira went below deck to save his camera equipment and drowned when the second blast hit. New Zealand police soon arrested 2 suspects posing as a honeymooning Swiss couple. They were actually agents of France's foreign intelligence service, the DGSE. France flatly denied it for months, until the Prime Minister admitted French agents had sunk the ship under orders. The Defense Minister resigned. The agents were sentenced to 10 years in prison, then transferred to a French Pacific atoll. Both were back home in France within about 2 years. France at least confessed. The entries staged attacks on themselves and pinned them on someone else. Welcome to the False Flag Lightning Round!

segments.titre: No. 20: the Mukden Incident (1931), Japan's false flag
segments.resume: On September 18, 1931, Kwantung Army officers blew up a bomb beside a Japanese-owned railway near Mukden without Tokyo's approval, blamed Chinese soldiers and invaded Manchuria, installing a puppet state. A League of Nations investigation rejected the self-defense claim and Japan simply quit the League.
segments.texte: 20. On the night of September 18th 1931, officers of Japan's Kwantung Army detonated a bomb beside a Japanese-owned railway near Mukden, in Manchuria. And it was done without approval from their own government in Tokyo. The Japanese army blamed Chinese soldiers and, within hours, launched an invasion. Just months later, Japan controlled all of Manchuria and had installed a puppet state. When a League of Nations investigation concluded the invasion couldn't be justified as self-defense, Japan's response was simply to quit the League. Eight years later, Nazi Germany borrowed the same playbook to start the war in Europe.

segments.titre: No. 19: the Gleiwitz incident that triggered World War II
segments.resume: On August 31, 1939, SS men in Polish uniforms attacked a German radio station at Gleiwitz, leaving the drugged and shot body of Franciszek Honiok dressed as a Polish raider. Hitler cited Polish attacks to invade Poland the next day, starting World War II; SS officer Alfred Naujocks later detailed the plot in a sworn statement.
segments.texte: 19. On the night of August 31st, 1939, SS men in Polish uniforms stormed a German radio station in the border town of Gleiwitz and broadcast a short anti-German message. Before they left, they dumped the body of a Polish-sympathizing German man named Franciszek Honiok who had been drugged and shot by the SS and dressed up to look like a Polish raider. The next morning, Hitler cited Polish attacks as the rationale for Germany’s invasion of Poland, and the Second World War officially began. The man who led the raid, SS officer Alfred Naujocks, laid out the whole plot in a sworn statement after the war. And Stalin was taking notes.

segments.titre: No. 18: the Shelling of Mainila, Stalin's pretext to invade Finland
segments.resume: On November 26, 1939 the USSR claimed Finnish artillery shelled the village of Mainila and killed four Red Army soldiers, though Finland had pulled its guns back and its border guards logged the shots as coming from the Soviet side. Four days later the USSR invaded Finland; historians broadly agree the shelling was staged.
segments.texte: 18. On November 26, 1939, the Soviets announced that Finnish artillery had shelled the border village of Mainila, killing 4 Red Army soldiers. The USSR demanded an apology. But there was one small problem. The Finnish army had already pulled its artillery back out of range of the border, specifically to avoid this kind of incident. Finnish border guards even logged the shots as coming from the Soviet side. None of that mattered. Evidence, as it turned out, was optional. 4 days later, the Soviet Union invaded Finland. Historians now broadly agree the shelling was staged by the Soviets themselves. The Finns then made the invasion spectacularly unpleasant, but that’s a topic for another time.

segments.titre: No. 17: Operation Ajax and the CIA's false flag in Iran
segments.resume: In 1953 the CIA and British intelligence overthrew Iran's Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh after he nationalized oil. According to the CIA's internal history, agents posing as Tudeh Party communists threatened clerics and staged a fake bombing of a cleric's home to turn the clergy against him. The Shah was restored and the CIA acknowledged its role only in 2013.
segments.texte: 17. How do you turn a country’s clergy against its prime minister? If you’re the CIA in 1953, you hire people to pretend to be communists and threaten them. 2 years earlier, Iran’s elected Prime Minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, nationalized the country's oil industry. It was controlled by a British company so London and Washington decided he had to go. Under Operation Ajax, the CIA and British intelligence set out to topple him, and one of their tools was a false flag. According to the CIA's own internal history, agents posing as members of Iran's Communist Tudeh Party threatened Muslim religious leaders. They even staged a fake bombing of a cleric's home, hoping to scare the clergy into turning against Mossadegh. And it worked. In August 1953, Mossadegh was overthrown and the Shah was restored to power. The CIA didn't officially acknowledge its role in the coup until 2013, 60 years later.

segments.titre: No. 16: the vanished uranium cargo of the Scheersberg A
segments.resume: In November 1968 the freighter Scheersberg A left Antwerp with 560 drums of uranium ore labeled PLUMBAT bound for Genoa and never arrived; it turned up in Turkey with a new crew, an empty hold and torn logbook pages. When the story broke in 1977 it emerged that Israeli intelligence used front companies and transferred the cargo at sea to fuel Israel's secret nuclear program.
segments.texte: 16. It’s hard to lose 200 tons of, well, anything. But in November 1968, a freighter called the Scheersberg A left Antwerp with 560 drums of uranium ore labeled "PLUMBAT," and was supposed to dock in Genoa, Italy. It never arrived. Weeks later, the ship turned up in a Turkish port with a different crew, an empty hold, and pages torn out of its logbook. For years, European nuclear regulators knew the uranium was gone but said nothing. When the story finally broke in 1977, the explanation was a heist straight out of a spy novel. Israeli intelligence had arranged the entire purchase through front companies, and the cargo was transferred at sea to an Israeli vessel to fuel the country's secret nuclear program. Time for some Human Guinea Pigs!

segments.titre: No. 15: human guinea pigs and sarin at Porton Down
segments.resume: For decades British servicemen were paid and given leave to join tests at the Porton Down chemical weapons lab, many believing they were helping cure the common cold. In May 1953 RAF engineer Ronald Maddison died after sarin was dripped on his arm; a secret inquest ruled misadventure, and only in 2004 did a new inquest find unlawful killing, followed by compensation for hundreds of veterans.
segments.texte: 15. Nobody at Porton Down saw nerve gas in the fine print of their terms and conditions of their stay at the UK’s top secret chemical weapons lab. For decades, British servicemen were offered extra pay and leave to take part in tests at Porton Down research facility in rural England. Many of them believed they were helping find a cure for the common cold. In May 1953, a 20-year-old RAF engineer named Ronald Maddison sat down for his test. Scientists dripped a trace amount of pure sarin nerve agent onto a patch of cloth on his arm. Maddison was dead within hours. The original inquest was held in secret and attributed the incident to “misadventure.” It took until 2004, more than 50 years later, and numerous complaints of experiment-related illnesses at the facility, for a new inquest to rule that Maddison had been unlawfully killed. The British government eventually paid compensation to hundreds of Porton Down veterans who were unwillingly subjected to experiments.

segments.titre: No. 14: Operation Big Buzz, the Army's mosquito bomb tests
segments.resume: In 1955 the Army Chemical Corps bred about a million yellow fever mosquitoes, loaded them into E14 cluster bombs and dropped them over Georgia; Operation Big Buzz released roughly 330,000. The mosquitoes carried no disease, but the tests showed they survived and still bit people up to 2,000 feet away; Operation Drop Kick (1956) and a 1958 Florida release followed.
segments.texte: 14. In 1955, the Army Chemical Corps bred about a million yellow fever mosquitoes, loaded them into E14 cluster bombs, and dropped them from 300 feet (91 meters) over Georgia. Operation Big Buzz sent roughly 330,000 of them out the hatch. They weren't carrying yellow fever, that would have been the wartime version. But the test was designed to ask 2 important questions. Can a mosquito survive being bombed? And will it still want dinner afterward? As it turns out, yes, and very much yes. Traps caught them up to 2,000 feet (610 meters) from the drop zone, feeding on humans and guinea pigs alike. The sequel, Operation Drop Kick, released even more over Savannah in 1956. Then, in 1958, the Army let a million loose over Avon Park, Florida.

segments.titre: No. 13: Project 112 and SHAD, chemical tests on Navy ships
segments.resume: Between 1962 and 1973 the Pentagon ran Project 112 and its naval branch SHAD, spraying Navy ships with nerve agents like VX and sarin and bacteria like E. coli (tests named Autumn Gold, Copper Head, Folded Arrow). Nearly 5,800 service members took part, many unaware, and the files stayed classified until 2000.
segments.texte: 13. Between 1962 and 1973, the Pentagon turned its own ships into test tubes as part of Project 112 and its naval branch, SHAD, or Shipboard Hazard Defense. Planes and boats sprayed Navy vessels with nerve agents like VX and sarin, and bacteria like E. coli to see how an attack would spread through a ship. The tests read like a Pentagon cologne line. Autumn Gold. Copper Head. Folded Arrow. Many of the nearly 5,800 service members involved had no idea they were in one. The files stayed classified until 2000. And while the Pentagon spent decades hiding SHAD, in 1991, it found something new to deny.

segments.titre: No. 12: the Khamisiyah demolition and Gulf War exposure
segments.resume: In March 1991, just after the Gulf War, US engineers blew up an Iraqi bunker and a rocket pit at Khamisiyah containing sarin and cyclosarin rockets. The Pentagon first concluded no troops were exposed, admitted the event in 1996 with an estimate of 98,900 troops under the plume, which exceeded 100,000 by 2000; auditors said its conclusions could not be supported.
segments.texte: 12. On March 4th, 1991, days after the Gulf War ended, U.S. combat engineers blew up an Iraqi ammunition bunker. Six 6 later, they blew up a pit of rockets next door for good measure. Inside were 122-millimeter rockets loaded with sarin and cyclosarin nerve agents. In October of the same year, UN inspectors found evidence of chemical weapons, but it wasn’t until 1993 that the Pentagon officially concluded that no troops had been exposed. It took until June 1996 to admit what happened. Its estimate of troops who may have been under the plume came to 98,900. By 2000, that number was over 100,000. Government auditors later ruled that the Pentagon's exposure conclusions could not be adequately supported. But if the Pentagon exposed its troops overseas by accident, in St. Louis, the Army sprayed American families on purpose…

segments.titre: No. 11: the Army's zinc cadmium sulfide spraying of St. Louis
segments.resume: In the 1950s and 60s the Army told St. Louis residents it was testing a smokescreen to hide the city from Soviet radar, but sprayed zinc cadmium sulfide from rooftops and station wagons to simulate a biological attack. A target area was a mostly Black slum district including Pruitt-Igoe; the Army says follow-up studies found no risk, while survivors cite health warnings and still seek compensation.
segments.texte: 11. The 1950s and 1960s were a wild time for military conspiracies, especially if you were a resident of St. Louis. If you were, you were told that the Army would be testing a smokescreen to hide the city from Soviet radar. Nobody thought to explain why hiding a city from radar required spraying its playgrounds. What actually came out of the blowers on rooftops and in the backs of station wagons was zinc cadmium sulfide, sprayed to simulate how a biological attack would spread. The Army's own records described one target area as a “densely populated slum district.” It was about 75% Black, and it included the Pruitt-Igoe housing project. The Army says follow-up studies found no health risk. But survivors point to a government study warning that repeated exposure could cause kidney and bone damage and lung cancer, and they're still fighting for compensation. If you thought that was bad, wait until you hear what Apartheid South Africa did.

segments.titre: No. 10 (part 1): Project Coast, apartheid South Africa's chemical and biological weapons program
segments.resume: In the 1980s apartheid South Africa's military built Project Coast, hidden behind front companies such as Delta G Scientific and Roodeplaat Research Laboratories. Labs worked on anthrax, cholera and nerve agents, and almost a fifth of projects concerned fertility, including contraceptive vaccines intended to secretly sterilize Black people.
segments.texte: 10. In the 1980s, apartheid South Africa’s military built a secret chemical and biological weapons program called Project Coast. It was hidden behind front companies with names like Delta G Scientific and Roodeplaat Research Laboratories. While the labs worked on anthrax, cholera, and nerve agents, almost a fifth of the projects were about fertility. The research involved fertility-control vaccines, adding an even more horrific dimension to this program. Those contraceptives would be given solely to black people to make them sterile without their knowing.

segments.titre: No. 10 (part 2): Wouter Basson, "Dr. Death", and his trial
segments.resume: Project Coast leader Wouter Basson, an army cardiologist, was accused of supplying poisons to kill anti-apartheid activists and was caught in 1997 trying to sell 100,000 ecstasy tablets. Tried on 67 charges including 16 murders, he saw the counts about some 200 deaths in Namibia thrown out for jurisdiction, and was acquitted in 2002.
segments.texte: As the program was uncovered, its leader, army cardiologist Wouter Basson, was accused of supplying poison slipped into tea, soft drinks, and beer to kill anti-apartheid activists. The program also mass-produced ecstasy, which is how Basson ended up in handcuffs. In 1997, narcotics agents caught him trying to sell 100,000 tablets. As they closed in, he dived into a dam in a futile attempt to escape. It didn’t work. He was tried on 67 charges, 16 of them murder. The judge threw out the counts covering some 200 deaths in Namibia, ruling that South African courts couldn't try crimes committed abroad. He called the rest of the prosecution's case too fragmented and confusing. So, in 2002, Dr. Death walked out of court acquitted. South Africa’s poison labs were kept secret on purpose. In the Soviet Union, the secret got out, literally, through an air filter.

segments.titre: No. 9: the 1979 Sverdlovsk anthrax leak
segments.resume: In April 1979 anthrax killed at least 64 people in Sverdlovsk, and Moscow blamed tainted black market meat while the KGB seized hospital records. The source was Compound 19, a military plant making anthrax spores, where workers had forgotten to replace an exhaust filter. In 1992 Matthew Meselson's team mapped victims along a downwind line and Yeltsin admitted military responsibility.
segments.texte: 9. In April 1979, people in the Soviet city of Sverdlovsk started dying of anthrax. At least 64 were killed. Moscow blamed tainted black market meat, and the KGB confiscated hospital records to keep that story straight. The real source was Compound 19, a military plant that made dried anthrax spores for weapons. According to a top Soviet bioweapons scientist who later defected, workers had simply forgotten to replace a filter on an exhaust system. In the long history of skipped maintenance, this one is hard to top. 13 years later in 1992, Harvard's Matthew Meselson and his team mapped where each victim had been that day. The victims fell along a straight line, directly downwind of the plant. That same year, Russian President Boris Yeltsin admitted the military was responsible. He would know. In 1979, he'd been Sverdlovsk's Communist Party boss. Meanwhile, NATO was busy hiding entire armies in Western Europe…

segments.titre: No. 8: Gladio and NATO's secret stay-behind armies
segments.resume: After World War II Western intelligence and NATO built secret stay-behind networks of trained civilians with buried weapons and explosives to resist a Soviet invasion. Italian Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti admitted the Italian branch, Gladio, to parliament in 1990, causing chaos amid probes into far-right links to bombings in the Years of Lead; the European Parliament condemned the networks.
segments.texte: 8. After World War II, Western intelligence agencies were worried that if the Soviets rolled into Western Europe, there'd be no one left to fight back. So, working with NATO, they built secret “stay-behind” networks in countries across the continent. They were composed of trained civilians and operatives with buried stashes of weapons and explosives. Think of it as a resistance movement, pre-assembled, with all the explosives and guns included. The public found out in 1990, when Italy’s Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti admitted to parliament that Italy's branch, called Gladio, had existed for decades. The revelation caused chaos, especially in Italy where investigators had already been examining links between far-right extremists and deadly bombings during the country's “Years of Lead.” The European Parliament passed a resolution condemning the networks and demanding full investigations. Fortunately, NATO's secret armies never had to fire a shot at the Soviets. In Northern Ireland, very public British soldiers fired on citizens, and then the government covered for them.

segments.titre: No. 7: Bloody Sunday and the Saville Report
segments.resume: On January 30, 1972 British paratroopers opened fire on a civil rights march in Derry, shooting 26 unarmed civilians, 14 of whom died. The Widgery inquiry largely cleared the soldiers and suggested victims had weapons; the 2010 Saville Report found none posed a threat and the killings unjustified, David Cameron apologized, and in 2025 the only soldier tried was acquitted.
segments.texte: 7. On January 30th, 1972, British paratroopers opened fire on a civil rights march in Derry, Northern Ireland. Twenty-six unarmed civilians were shot. 14 of them died. An official inquiry led by Lord Widgery largely cleared the soldiers just 11 weeks later. He also suggested some of the victims had been handling guns or nail bombs. In 1998, the government opened a new inquiry. It took 12 years and cost nearly £200 million to finalize, roughly £5 million for every year of denial. But in 2010, the Saville Report concluded that none of the victims had posed any threat and that the killings were unjustified and unjustifiable. Then Prime Minister David Cameron stood up in Parliament and apologized, and in 2025, the only soldier ever brought to trial over the Bloody Sunday killings was acquitted. Britain spent almost four decades protecting its own soldiers, after World War II, but the U.S. protected someone else’s…. including some of the worst war criminals of the century.

segments.titre: No. 6: Unit 731 and the US immunity deal
segments.resume: Japan's Unit 731 in occupied China, under General Shiro Ishii, infected prisoners with plague, cholera and anthrax, performed vivisections and dropped plague-infected fleas on Chinese cities. After the war American officials granted immunity in exchange for the research, no leaders faced trial in Tokyo, and the US dismissed the 1949 Soviet trial of Unit 731 members as propaganda.
segments.texte: 6. In occupied China, Japan’s Unit 731 famously ran some of the worst experimental programs of the 20th century. Under General Shiro Ishii, doctors infected prisoners with plague, cholera, and anthrax, performed vivisections on living people, and dropped plague-infected fleas over Chinese cities. Thousands died inside the facility itself, and far more died in the field attacks. After the war, American officials made a deal: immunity in exchange for their research on biological weapons. None of the unit's leaders faced a war crimes trial in Tokyo, and several went on to comfortable careers in Japanese medicine and business. When the Soviets put a handful of Unit 731 members on trial in 1949, the US dismissed it as communist propaganda. Hiding someone else's war crimes is bad. But the Soviets managed to blame their own massacre on the Nazis, and nearly got away with it at Nuremberg…

segments.titre: No. 5: the Katyn massacre and the Soviet cover-up
segments.resume: In spring 1940 the Soviet secret police shot about 22,000 Polish officers, police and professionals on Stalin's order. After Germany found the Katyn graves in 1943 Moscow blamed the Nazis, tried to add it to the Nuremberg charges, and the US and Britain buried evidence; the USSR admitted NKVD responsibility in 1990, and in 2010 a plane crash killed Poland's president en route to the Katyn memorial.
segments.texte: 5. In the spring of 1940, the Soviet secret police rounded up about 22,000 Polish army officers, police, doctors, lawyers, and teachers and shot them. Most were killed with a single bullet to the back of the head. The order had been signed by Stalin himself. When German troops discovered the mass graves in Katyn Forest in 1943, Moscow blamed the Nazis. The Soviets even tried to add Katyn to the list of German crimes at the Nuremberg trials. Meanwhile, the US and British governments, not wanting to anger a wartime ally, buried their own evidence pointing at Moscow. The lie survived until April 1990, when the Soviet Union admitted the NKVD was responsible. And in 2010, the story added one last cruel twist. Poland's president and dozens of the country's top officials died in a plane crash on their way to the 70th anniversary memorial at Katyn.

segments.titre: No. 4: the Nayirah incubator testimony before the Gulf War
segments.resume: In October 1990 a tearful 15-year-old identified as Nayirah told a US congressional caucus that Iraqi soldiers pulled babies from incubators in Kuwait. Bush and senators repeated it before a Senate war vote that passed by five votes. In 1992 it emerged she was the Kuwaiti ambassador's daughter, coached via PR firm Hill & Knowlton paid by Citizens for a Free Kuwait, and no credible evidence supported the story.
segments.texte: 4. In October 1990, two months after Iraq invaded Kuwait, a tearful 15-year-old girl identified only as Nayirah testified before a US congressional caucus. She said she'd watched Iraqi soldiers pull premature babies out of hospital incubators in Kuwait before “leaving them to die on the cold floor.” President George H.W. Bush repeated it again and again. Several senators cited it in the debate before the vote to authorize war, a vote that passed the Senate by just five votes. In 1992, it came out that Nayirah was the daughter of Kuwait's ambassador to the United States. Her testimony had been arranged by the PR giant Hill & Knowlton, which was paid millions by a Kuwaiti government-backed group called Citizens for a Free Kuwait. Later investigations found no credible evidence the incubator story ever happened. Congress had been moved to tears by a client pitch. Faking a story to start a war is bad. Faking one about your own dead hero, then lying to his family, somehow feels even worse…

segments.titre: No. 3: Pat Tillman's friendly-fire death and the Army cover-up
segments.resume: NFL player Pat Tillman left the Arizona Cardinals to become an Army Ranger after 9/11 and was killed in Afghanistan on April 22, 2004. The Army said he died charging enemy fighters and gave him a Silver Star, but he was killed by fellow Rangers; officials knew almost immediately, burned his gear, and kept his family in the dark for over a month, drawing censure of several officers including four generals.
segments.texte: 3. Pat Tillman turned down a multimillion-dollar NFL contract with the Arizona Cardinals to become an Army Ranger after 9/11. The Army repaid him by turning his death into a recruiting poster. It was extremely patriotic, and much publicized. On April 22nd, 2004, Tillman had paid the ultimate sacrifice and was killed in Afghanistan. The Army told the public and his family he died charging up a hill at enemy fighters, and awarded him a Silver Star for heroism. In reality, Tillman had been killed by his fellow Rangers in a friendly-fire accident… And the Army knew it almost immediately. Soldiers burned his uniform and body armor. A general sent a memo warning top officials that it was highly possible Tillman had died from friendly fire, so that the President wouldn't unknowingly repeat the heroic version in a speech. Nobody thought to send that memo to his family. Meanwhile, they sat through a nationally televised memorial built on the fake story. They weren't told the truth for more than a month. Pentagon investigators later faulted several senior officers, including 4 generals, for how it was handled.

segments.titre: No. 2: North Korea's abduction of Japanese citizens
segments.resume: On November 15, 1977 13-year-old Megumi Yokota vanished walking home in Niigata, one of many Japanese people who disappeared from the west coast; those blaming North Korea were dismissed as conspiracy theorists. In 2002 Kim Jong-il admitted to abducting 13 citizens to train spies, five returned, and DNA tests showed remains given for Megumi belonged to someone else; Japan recognizes 17 abductees.
segments.texte: 2. On November 15, 1977, a 13-year-old Japanese girl named Megumi Yokota walked home from badminton practice in the coastal city of Niigata. She never arrived. For years, Japanese people kept vanishing from beaches along the country's western coast. Some people pointed the finger squarely at North Korea, but were written off as conspiracy theorists. Then, in 2002, North Korean leader Kim Jong-il sat down with Japan's Prime Minister and admitted that North Korean agents had abducted 13 Japanese citizens several decades before. Some were used to teach spies how to speak and act Japanese. 5 were allowed to return home. North Korea claimed the rest, including Megumi, were dead. When Pyongyang later handed over remains it said were hers, Japanese DNA testing concluded they belonged to someone else. Japan officially recognizes 17 abductees today. Our number one entry is the conspiracy theory that ate itself…

segments.titre: No. 1: Operation INFEKTION, the KGB's AIDS disinformation campaign
segments.resume: In 1983 a pro-Soviet Indian newspaper printed an anonymous letter claiming AIDS was a Pentagon bioweapon; a Soviet paper repeated it in 1985 and the Stasi pushed a pseudo-scientific report blaming Fort Detrick. The story spread to media in over 80 countries as part of the KGB's Operation INFEKTION, admitted by Yevgeny Primakov in 1992, and is still repeated today.
segments.texte: 1. In 1983, a small pro-Soviet newspaper in India printed an anonymous letter from an allegedly well-known American scientist. It claimed that AIDS, a terrifying new disease at the time, had been created by the Pentagon as a biological weapon. In 1985, a Soviet newspaper repeated the claim and cited the Indian article as its source. East Germany's secret police, the Stasi, then helped push a pseudo-scientific report blaming the Army's biological research lab at Fort Detrick, Maryland. Within a few years, the story had run in the media in more than 80 countries. The whole thing was a part of Operation INFEKTION, a KGB disinformation campaign built to turn the world against the US military. In 1992, the head of Russia's foreign intelligence service, Yevgeny Primakov, admitted the KGB had been behind it. The story had a life of its own, and it's still repeated today. So the craziest military conspiracy on this list is one that never happened, invented by a very real conspiracy that did.
